title: Huawei's Ascend chose the hardest road: not compatible with Nvidia
dek: For three or four decades Chinese IT has been a follower industry. Ascend is Huawei's first product that does not solve a chokehold problem but instead goes voluntarily into uncharted territory, starting at the same time as Nvidia. Xu Zhijun said: anything you do as a follower gets harder and harder the longer you do it.
why: The first half is about how the book was written, with low information density; from the two key decisions at Ascend's project launch onward, Fang Xingdong gives a lot of frontline detail and judgment that only exists in the book.
who: Founders, investors and engineers watching domestic compute, the semiconductor supply chain and AI infrastructure, especially those who want to understand the difference between Ascend's route and Nvidia's.
skip: The first ~13 minutes cover the origins of the six books and the interview process, with little bearing on investment judgment.

points.h: Ascend's harshest decision was not being compatible with Nvidia
points.body: At project launch Ascend faced two choices. The first was whether AI chips should be specialized or general-purpose; Liao Heng, as chief scientist, judged that AI should be a general-purpose product, and the architectural choice has been proven right today. The second was harder: whether to be compatible with Nvidia. Many domestic chips choose compatibility, because the benefit is that Nvidia's existing ecosystem and tools can all be shared. But Xu Zhijun was firm from the start that they had to take a different path. Fang Xingdong thinks this choice took enormous nerve at the time, and that it faced huge challenges many times along the way — because the entire Chinese IT industry has been a follower industry for three or four decades, and has never developed on the basis of its own root technology.

points.h: Anything you do as a follower gets harder and harder
points.body: Fang Xingdong recalls having dinner with Xu Zhijun three years ago, when Xu half muttered to himself: Huawei has done this for so many years, and the discovery is that anything you do as a follower always gets harder and harder the longer you do it. There are two kinds of following. In standardized products, Chinese companies can always close the gap and even overtake — but by the time they overtake, there is no profit left in the industry; 2G to 5G, PCs and phones were all like this. In non-standardized products, such as routers competing with Cisco for so many years, the gap has not closed. In Xu Zhijun's eyes, what Huawei did in the past was also following. That is why Ascend is special among the six products: the other five solve chokehold problems and address survival first, whereas Ascend was not choked in 2019 — it is a fully proactive compute product.

points.h: With process choked off, only system innovation can make it back
points.body: Each generation of industry chips gains roughly 20% or more in performance, mainly from the increase in transistor count driven by advanced process improvements. Huawei lost that premise and can only gain performance through system innovation and breakthroughs — stacked compute, interconnect, higher integration. Fang Xingdong explains with a car metaphor: before, you just had to make the engine stronger and stronger; now the engine is constrained and cannot be enlarged, so you can only make the car run well through architecture, weight reduction and cooling. Nvidia's answer is to keep working on the engine, because TSMC can still manufacture it. In the interview Liao Heng uses the metaphor of an 18-story pagoda: many companies are good at only one layer because of the great division of labor, while Huawei is forced to do manufacturing, ecosystem and chip design all at once.

points.h: Huawei has to pull the domestic supply chain up with it
points.body: In the past Huawei did design, relied on the global supply chain, had TSMC manufacture, could pick the best international partners for other components, buy American products and assemble them, sell at a good price with a brand premium, and still make decent profit. Now it cannot cooperate with foreign partners, TSMC cannot process for it, and domestic processes are still lacking in every respect, so Huawei has no choice but to support and pull up the domestic supply chain — only then does it have a way to survive, only then can its products be manufactured. So the challenge of the past seven years is not just improving its own capabilities but also pulling the entire supply chain up — without that, independent self-reliance is impossible. Manufacturing is not Huawei's main business, but it has to help companies like SMIC and Yangtze Memory keep advancing process, yield and quality.

points.h: Ascend's significance is not that Huawei survived, but that the industry has an engine
points.body: In the past, Huawei's product launches and iterations were still based on American root technology and the industry ecosystem; the high-value components of a phone were basically foreign. Now Huawei's phones, including Ascend, almost 100% pull up the domestic supply chain. Fang Xingdong believes the greatest significance of the Tao Law is not that Huawei itself can survive and be self-reliant, but that China's entire semiconductor industry and entire IT industry now has its own engine, which never existed before. Huawei's rapid development represents the rapid development of the entire industry ecosystem. He also points out that the market, reading reports, news or public opinion, has not yet realized that we are at this inflection point in the cycle — people mention Nvidia and think it is formidable, and mention Huawei and say it is policy that makes everyone use it.

points.h: It is not a question of difficulty, but of cognition and resolve
points.body: Fang Xingdong believes doing communications versus doing IT is essentially not a question of difficulty but of cognition and resolve — whether you dare to do it. The most typical example is the Gauss database: among these six products Ascend stood out, and the least conspicuous is probably Gauss, but the database is a half-century-old industry with a fairly stable market, and if it really gets choked it is deadly. At the time Huawei wanted to acquire or support a domestic vendor, but after research found that none of them were up to it; domestic companies could only grow in the cracks left by American giants, with small scale, weak R&D capability and weak product innovation. So Huawei decided to do it itself, benchmarking Oracle, investing 1 billion, 2 billion, 3 billion yuan a year starting in 2011 and 2012, without knowing whether there would ever be output.

points.h: The future is two centers, not one replacing the other
points.body: Fang Xingdong judges that the shift of global high tech from a single system centered on the US to two centers is the general trend; politics will not allow a continued single center — the US will not allow it, and China will not allow it either. He believes a single center is itself abnormal, and only two centers can create competition — only with two systems does every consumer, every company and every country, large or small, have a choice, and not be forced to pick one of two under a chokehold. So the mission of Huawei's six products is to go from being the second choice to being the better choice; the relationship with Nvidia is not simple substitution but each having its strengths, complementing each other, and co-opetition. He admits the American system is currently stronger, with its advantage mainly in advanced manufacturing, and that Huawei, under process constraints, uses the Tao Law to avoid being left behind; once advanced process is also broken through, it can work both tracks at once.

points.h: The tech war won in the short term, at a greater long-term cost
points.body: Fang Xingdong believes the US did indeed suppress Huawei through the tech war, but cannot solve the problem in the long term. He reasons: without the national confrontation of 2017 and 2018, Huawei might be at least one-third of Nvidia, one-third of Apple, and possibly China's largest company by market cap; in 2019 Huawei had already surpassed Apple, and its global shipments briefly surpassed Samsung for one quarter. Nvidia is dominant today, but if it had been running neck and neck with Huawei in AI chips from the start, it could not have reached this position today. He judges that once the side being attacked builds a self-cycle that does not rely on the outside, and the other side cannot eliminate it even under the harshest conditions, it will be even harder to eliminate later; it will only grow stronger, turning a monopoly into a duopoly.

terms.term: Tao Law / system-level performance improvement path
terms.def: When process is constrained, trading architecture, interconnect, packaging and other system optimizations for chip performance gains.

terms.term: Red Army Blue Army / Huawei's internal adversarial decision mechanism
terms.def: An internal mechanism that sets up pro and con sides to debate the same decision, used for strategy and solution validation.

terms.term: Hardware-software co-design / joint chip and model design
terms.def: Compute companies and model companies communicate in advance about next-generation features and define the product together.

quotes.text: He said Huawei has done this for so many years, and the discovery is that anything you do as a follower always gets harder and harder the longer you do it.
I have been in this industry for 30 years, and I feel that a lot of my past understanding can be reset to zero.
Without the tech war, Huawei is an excellent company, but it might not, would not become a great company; but with the tech war, it will certainly become a great company.

So the few hurdles Huawei faces now are really about technology, but what it drives is the upgrading of China's entire industry, the entire supply chain — yet many things it has to do itself first, because if it does not do them, no one else can.
Once the side being attacked, whether Huawei or China, builds a self-cycle, a self-cycle that does not rely on the outside, frankly it becomes a long-term competitor.
